As fine as needles and packed densely, too numerous to count. 

In the Song dynasty, grass carp made up a significant portion of freshwater fish farming. People dug ponds, constructed buildings beside them, and often cultivated economic crops like lotus root, gorgon fruit, and wild rice, creating an ideal environment for fish to thrive. They would then release fry as fine as needles into the ponds and raise them with great care. Some fry were too tiny to count accurately, so the ancients inserted bamboo markers and used portioning methods to gauge the density of fry in a container. This shows that measurement tools for counting fry already existed in the Song dynasty.

Burial is concealment, harnessing the vital energy.  

The qi of yin and yang, exhaled, becomes wind; rising, becomes clouds; descending, becomes rain; flowing beneath the earth, becomes vital energy. Life is the gathering of qi. When condensed, it forms bones, which remain after death. Thus, burial reverses qi to absorb the bones, nurturing the path of the living. As the scripture says: Qi resonates and responds, and the blessings of the dead reach the living.  

...  

When placing stone lions at the tomb gate, their heads must face the Gate of Life, and their tails sweep the path of the underworld. With their eyes fixed on the yang realm, malevolent spirits dare not intrude; with their claws firmly planted, the deceased rest in peace. If their positions are reversed, the yang passage will be blocked, yin energy will stagnate, and the flow of vitality will cease.
